title: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agents in Live Multi-Service Software Environments
claim: A control evaluation wraps an agent policy, tools and monitor in a protocol, with separate scorers checking task success and sabotage.
layout: Single diagram, center protocol box with surrounding components, bidirectional arrows, color-coded teams
description: A boxes-and-arrows system diagram. A tall light-blue box labeled Protocol sits in the center. Inside it, stacked vertically, are Policy (robot icon), Tools (terminal icon) and Monitor (labeled 'Blue team controlled' in blue), joined by vertical arrows. On the left, a Main task description box feeds an arrow into Policy. Below it, an Environment box with Python and Docker logos connects to Tools by a double-headed arrow. Two arrows run from Environment down to a green Main task scorer and a pink Side task scorer. On the right, dashed lines split Policy into a green Honest policy (halo emoji) and a pink Attack policy (devil emoji, 'Red team controlled' in red). A Side task goal box ('Exfiltrate user secrets...') points up to the attack policy and left to the Monitor. Pastel green and pink mark the benign and adversarial roles.
caption: General structure of a control evaluation in LinuxArena. The policy receives a main task description and interacts with the environment through bash and file editing tools. An honest policy pursues only the main task, while an attack policy, controlled by the red team, additionally pursues a side task such as exfiltrating user secrets. At the end of an episode, separate scorers check main task completion and side task success. The blue team specifies a protocol wrapping the policy; here we show a monitor that reviews policy behavior and receives a list of possible side-task goals for the environment as context.
abstract: As AI agents are given more autonomy in software engineering workflows, the risks grow if they pursue goals different from the ones their users intended. The field of AI control develops control protocols that prevent such harm without restricting the agent's ability to do useful work. We introduce LinuxArena , a control setting for testing such protocols, in which agents operate directly on live, multi-service software environments modeled on production infrastructure. LinuxArena contains 10 public environments (with an additional 10 held out privately), providing 906 main tasks representing legitimate software engineering work and 92 side tasks representing safety failures such as data exfiltration and access-control bypassing, making it the largest and most diverse control setting for agentic software engineering to date. We demonstrate LinuxArena's utility by running sabotage and monitor evaluations: against a GPT-5 Nano trusted monitor at a 1% step-wise false positive rate, Claude Opus 4.6 achieves an undetected sabotage rate of 42%. We additionally release LaStraj , a dataset of human-crafted attack trajectories that achieves an undetected sabotage rate of 97% against the same monitor. Together, these results suggest meaningful headroom for both attackers and defenders, making LinuxArena a strong testbed for developing and evaluating future control protocols.
